No, it does not use a database transaction. According to [[write-journal]], the rollback mechanism is implemented entirely through an **in-memory journal** that records the prior state of files before they are written. If a run fails, it rolls back every recorded write in reverse order by restoring previous content or deleting newly created files.

The page explicitly states: "This approach provides all-or-nothing write semantics without requiring a database transaction — the in-memory journal itself acts as the transaction log for the duration of a single run."

So the journal itself serves as the transaction mechanism, not a separate database.
